3. SGLT2 Inhibitors: Empagliﬂozin
Empagliﬂozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitor. It inhibits the SGLT2 protein in
the proximal tubule of the kidney, which reduces reabsorption of ﬁltered glucose and increases
urinary glucose excretion. Empagliﬂozin lowers HbA1c, body weight and blood pressure.
Beyond glucose lowering, empagliﬂozin reduces cardiovascular death in patients with Type 2
Diabetes and established cardiovascular disease, and reduces hospitalization for heart failure. It also
slows the progression of chronic kidney disease. The ADA Standards of Care recommend an SGLT2
inhibitor for patients with Type 2 Diabetes who have heart failure or chronic kidney disease.

•  Genital mycotic infections are the most common adverse eﬀect.
•  Urinary tract infections.
•  Volume depletion and hypotension, particularly in elderly patients and those taking diuretics.
•  Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis is rare but serious; empagliﬂozin should be stopped before
major surgery and during acute illness.

substantial weight loss and reduces major adverse cardiovascular events in patients with established

1. Hypertension
Hypertension is a persistent elevation of arterial blood pressure. The ACC/AHA hypertension
guideline deﬁnes hypertension as a blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg or higher and recommends a
treatment target below 130/80 mmHg for most adults. Hypertension is usually asymptomatic, which is
why it is often called a silent disease; very high blood pressure can cause headache, dizziness and
blurred vision.
Untreated hypertension causes stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, chronic kidney disease
and hypertensive retinopathy. Hypertension aﬀects the heart (left ventricular hypertrophy), the
kidneys, the brain and the eyes.
First-line drug classes are ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), calcium channel
blockers and thiazide diuretics. Many patients need two or more drugs.
2. ACE Inhibitors: Lisinopril
Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. It inhibits ACE, reducing the
production of angiotensin II, which causes vasodilation and reduced aldosterone secretion. Lisinopril
treats hypertension and heart failure. Lisinopril is recommended for patients with diabetes who have
albuminuria, because it slows the progression of diabetic nephropathy.
2.1 Adverse eﬀects
•  A dry, persistent cough occurs in up to 10 percent of patients, caused by accumulation of
bradykinin.
•  Hyperkalemia, because reduced aldosterone decreases potassium excretion.
•  Angioedema is rare but potentially life-threatening.
•  An initial rise in serum creatinine.
2.2 Contraindications
Lisinopril is contraindicated in pregnancy because it causes fetal kidney damage, and in patients with
a history of angioedema. Lisinopril should not be combined with an ARB such as losartan, because
dual blockade increases hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury without improving outcomes.

4. Calcium Channel Blockers: Amlodipine
Amlodipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker that relaxes arterial smooth muscle.
Amlodipine treats hypertension and stable angina. Its main adverse eﬀects are peripheral edema
(ankle swelling), headache and ﬂushing. Amlodipine does not aﬀect potassium levels.
5. Thiazide Diuretics: Hydrochlorothiazide
Hydrochlorothiazide inhibits sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubule. It treats
hypertension. Adverse eﬀects include hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hyperuricemia that can trigger
gout, and mild hyperglycemia. Hydrochlorothiazide should be used with caution in patients with a
history of gout.
6. Beta-Blockers: Metoprolol
Metoprolol is a cardioselective beta-1 blocker. It treats hypertension, angina and heart failure, and is
used for heart rate control in atrial ﬁbrillation. Adverse eﬀects include bradycardia, fatigue and cold
extremities. Metoprolol should be avoided in patients with second-degree or third-degree heart block.
7. Atrial Fibrillation
Atrial ﬁbrillation is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia. Symptoms include palpitations,
shortness of breath, fatigue and dizziness. Atrial ﬁbrillation causes blood to pool in the left atrium,
where clots can form; the main complication of atrial ﬁbrillation is ischemic stroke. Hypertension is the
most common risk factor for atrial ﬁbrillation.
Stroke risk is estimated with the CHA2DS2-VASc score, and patients with an elevated score are
treated with an anticoagulant. Options are warfarin or a direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban.
8. Warfarin
Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant. Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase
(VKORC1), which prevents activation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X. Warfarin prevents stroke in
atrial ﬁbrillation and treats deep vein thrombosis. Therapy is monitored with the INR, with a target
range of 2.0 to 3.0 for atrial ﬁbrillation.

1. Overview of Type 2 Diabetes
Type 2 Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease characterized by insulin resistance in muscle, liver
and adipose tissue, combined with progressive loss of insulin secretion by pancreatic beta cells. The
result is persistent hyperglycemia. Common symptoms include polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue and
blurred vision, although many patients are asymptomatic at diagnosis and are identiﬁed through
routine HbA1c screening.
Long-term hyperglycemia damages small and large blood vessels. Microvascular complications
include diabetic retinopathy, diabetic nephropathy and peripheral neuropathy. Macrovascular
complications include coronary artery disease, stroke and peripheral artery disease. Type 2 Diabetes
also leads to chronic kidney disease, and diabetic nephropathy is a leading cause of end-stage renal
disease.
Treatment combines lifestyle change (diet, physical activity, weight reduction) with glucose-lowering
drugs. Drug choice depends on cardiovascular risk, kidney function, risk of hypoglycemia, eﬀect on
body weight and cost.
2. Metformin
Metformin is the ﬁrst-line drug treatment for most adults with Type 2 Diabetes. It is a biguanide that
reduces hepatic glucose production (gluconeogenesis) and improves insulin sensitivity. At the
molecular level, metformin activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an energy-sensing
enzyme that inhibits gluconeogenesis in the liver.
2.1 Adverse eﬀects
•  Gastrointestinal eﬀects are the most common: nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort and a
metallic taste. Starting with a low dose and using extended-release tablets reduces them.
•  Long-term use can cause vitamin B12 deﬁciency; periodic B12 measurement is advised,
especially in patients with peripheral neuropathy.
•  Lactic acidosis is rare but serious, and occurs mainly when metformin accumulates because of
severe renal impairment.

Hypertension and Atrial Fibrillation: A Clinical Review
Synthetic educational document created for testing a retrieval system. Not clinical guidance.
1. Hypertension
Hypertension is a persistent elevation of arterial blood pressure. The ACC/AHA hypertension
guideline deﬁnes hypertension as a blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg or higher and recommends a
treatment target below 130/80 mmHg for most adults. Hypertension is usually asymptomatic, which is
why it is often called a silent disease; very high blood pressure can cause headache, dizziness and
blurred vision.
Untreated hypertension causes stroke, myocardial infarction, heart failure, chronic kidney disease
and hypertensive retinopathy. Hypertension aﬀects the heart (left ventricular hypertrophy), the
kidneys, the brain and the eyes.
First-line drug classes are ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs), calcium channel
blockers and thiazide diuretics. Many patients need two or more drugs.
2. ACE Inhibitors: Lisinopril
Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor. It inhibits ACE, reducing the
production of angiotensin II, which causes vasodilation and reduced aldosterone secretion. Lisinopril
treats hypertension and heart failure. Lisinopril is recommended for patients with diabetes who have
albuminuria, because it slows the progression of diabetic nephropathy.

•  A dry, persistent cough occurs in up to 10 percent of patients, caused by accumulation of

•  Angioedema is rare but potentially life-threatening.
•  An initial rise in serum creatinine.

Lisinopril is contraindicated in pregnancy because it causes fetal kidney damage, and in patients with
